title: Rafi and the Phishing Scare
markdown:
Sunbeams burst through Rafi’s window. His alarm buzzed; he was already awake. A buzzing energy, like a secret waiting. Feet hit the carpet. Toast drifted from downstairs. His mind was already on blinking lights and clever contraptions.

A frantic chirping. Cora, his jackdaw, zipped to the sill, feathers ruffled, a tiny storm. Dark eyes darted. “Squawk. Big trouble. Big trouble.” Whistles and clicks.

Rafi dashed to his tablet. Heart skip-hop. The school network homepage plastered with flashing garish signs. URGENT! Your account needs updating NOW! Chunky red letters that practically vibrated. Another, dazzling blue: CLAIM YOUR FREE PRIZE! Click HERE!

“What’s happening?” Fingers flying. The digital library — usually full of facts — flickered and died. A stark white box: Enter your password to proceed. School logo. Something off. A tiny buzz of wrongness.

Cora hopped onto the desk, pecked the flashing text. “Shiny. But wobbly text. Bad sparkle.” Tiny claws tap-tap. She loved shiny things and noticed everything: bent twigs, ripe berry colours.

“Wobbly text. Bad sparkle.” A thought. Fake shiny pebbles at the market — good from far away, up close dull stones with glitter glued on. Fonts a little crooked. Colours too loud. “Not a real update. Bait. Someone is trying to trick us.”

Ms. Lin, the principal, burst in, sensible shoes tapping fast. “Rafi. The school computers are acting strange. Files scrambled. Students locked out.”

“A network scare. Cora noticed. These messages are a trap. They want passwords.”

Lin’s brow furrowed. “Why?”

“To get to everything. Fishing for secrets. Wobbly text, bad sparkle — signs it’s not real. They’re trying to phish.”

“Phishing. A fake worm to catch a fish. We need a better shield. A password that’s a secret fort.”

Rafi’s eyes gleamed. “Super-strong passwords. Mix letters, numbers, symbols. A secret code. And teach everyone to spot the fake bait. Cora, password lookout.”

Cora puffed. “Always watching for wobbly text. Shiny deception.”

They made a thorough plan. Rafi coded a tighter filter that flagged the crooked fonts and the shouty colours. Lin gathered students. “Phishing is a trick. Fake messages, a shiny lure, hoping you’ll give away private information. Rafi and Cora helped us see the trap. Your password is a key. Long. Mixed. Never share it because a box asked nicely. If you see bad sparkle or wobbly text, don’t click.”

Rafi grinned at Cora. The network hummed back. The scare had been a lesson, a bit of digital danger tackled together.

He did not declare them explorers or start an adventure. He wrote the filter rules on a card by the lab machines, let Cora keep a screenshot of the worst banner as a trophy of ugliness, and ate the toast that had gone cold, which tasted like a morning that had done its job.
